T-RoPE: Time-Aware Rotary Position Embedding for Sequential Recommendation

Yang Liu   Noel Loo   Ali Khanafer   Shuying Sun   Akshay Soni Affiliation: Shopify Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Liquid AI    Zhong Wu   Linjun Yang Affiliation: Shopify
Abstract

Large-scale recommenders increasingly adopt the sequential generative recipe behind large language models, bringing the Transformer into recommendation along with design choices made for text, including Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE). In language models, RoPE encodes token indices for relative position reasoning, but in recommendation, an interaction index records only event order, saying nothing about elapsed time, behavioral cycles across scales, or calendar phase. We revisit this choice and propose T-RoPE, a time-aware RoPE for sequential generative recommendation that replaces index-only rotation with timestamp-based angles, learnable temporal coefficients, multiscale frequency banks, shifted query alignment, and non-stationary key rotation. We prove that standard RoPE, even on timestamps, remains time-translation invariant and cannot distinguish seasonal contexts, and that T-RoPE breaks this invariance while preserving the RoPE interface. Across five public benchmarks, T-RoPE achieves the best result on every metric on every dataset, improving over the strongest baseline by 78–130% in HR@10 on the sparse PixelRec data and 8–12% across metrics on Amazon Books. On an industrial-scale e-commerce dataset with more than 6B interactions, it improves every metric over the HSTU + Time RAB backbone by 13–82%, with ablations attributing the largest gains to multiscale frequencies (+56%+56\% NDCG@50) and non-stationary keys (+4%+4\%). An online A/B test in the Shop app yields positive lifts in conversion rate (+0.33%+0.33\%) and order count (+0.63%+0.63\%). We also provide forward and backward algorithms whose added cost is linear in sequence length and head dimension, keeping time-aware RoPE practical for large generative recommenders.

1 Introduction

Large language models have made autoregressive sequence modeling a practical way to learn from long, heterogeneous histories (Vaswani et al., 2017; Touvron et al., 2023). Their success comes not from the architecture alone but from a mature engineering stack of scalable training, fast attention kernels, and long-context modeling that makes generative prediction practical at scale. Recommendation models are now borrowing this recipe. Recent sequential generative recommenders represent user behavior as action sequences and autoregressively predict future items, actions, or semantic identifiers  (Rajput et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2025; OneRec Team and others, 2026; Liang et al., 2026). This recipe has already proven itself at production scale, where HSTU drives live recommendation systems on industrial workloads (Zhai et al., 2024).

This transfer is productive but imperfect, because inductive biases that serve language do not always carry over to recommendation. Generative recommenders inherit components from language models, including RoPE (Su et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Movahedi et al., 2026). RoPE injects sequence order by rotating query and key vectors according to an integer position index. For text, this is a natural coordinate, because token offsets carry much of the structure attention needs. For recommendation, the same coordinate loses what matters. An interaction index records that one event preceded another, but not whether the gap was seconds, weeks, or seasons.

This positional encoding gap leaves three temporal signals unrepresented. First, true time gaps are erased. A key six months in the past can be positionally identical to a key from yesterday if their sequence offsets match. Second, multiscale periodicity is absent. User behavior contains hourly, weekly, monthly, and seasonal rhythms, but index-based RoPE has no wall-clock frequency structure. Third, absolute calendar phase is inaccessible. Because index-based attention depends only on the relative offset m−nm-n, it is time-translation invariant. The same history evaluated at different points in a seasonal cycle produces the same attention pattern.

Existing temporal recommendation methods close only part of this gap, as Table 1 summarizes. TiSASRec injects discretized time-interval features into self-attention, which captures recency but not continuous multiscale periodicity or calendar phase (Li et al., 2020). HSTU adds a time-based Relative Attention Bias (RAB), mapping bucketed time gaps to a learned scalar added to the attention logits, which sharpens recency weighting but leaves the query and key geometry untouched and still discretizes time (Zhai et al., 2024). TO-RoPE brings timestamps into RoPE angles, but the joint geometry of its queries and keys remains time-translation invariant (Wei et al., 2025). As we prove in Section 4, it captures temporal distance but cannot distinguish queries issued in different calendar phases over the same history. Time cannot just sit alongside RoPE as an extra feature or bias, because closing the gap requires structurally changing the way RoPE itself rotates queries and keys.

To address this gap, we propose T-RoPE (Time-aware RoPE), a RoPE-compatible positional encoding for timestamped user histories. T-RoPE keeps the efficient RoPE interface but replaces index-only rotation with timestamp-based angles, learnable temporal coefficients, multiscale frequency banks, shifted query alignment, and non-stationary key rotation, as shown in Table 1. We list our main contributions below.

  1. 1.

    A time-aware RoPE for generative recommendation. T-RoPE encodes continuous timestamps directly in rotary attention to represent elapsed time, multiscale periodicity, and calendar phase within a single rotary encoding. Index-based RoPE discards these signals, and prior temporal encodings capture them only in part.

  2. 2.

    Theoretical analysis. We prove that rotating queries and keys by the same function of their timestamps yields time-translation invariant attention (covering standard RoPE on timestamps and TO-RoPE’s timestamp component), and that T-RoPE’s non-stationary key provably breaks this invariance.

  3. 3.

    Results across settings. On five public benchmarks, an industrial dataset with more than 6B interactions, and an online A/B test in the Shop app, T-RoPE improves over temporal and RoPE-based baselines on every public benchmark and delivers positive production lifts.

  4. 4.

    An efficient implementation path. We provide forward and backward algorithms and a cost analysis showing only linear overhead in sequence length and head dimension.

2 Preliminaries

In generative recommendation, the model input is a user’s interaction history, a sequence of timestamped events {(i1,t1),…,(iL,tL)}\{(i_{1},t_{1}),\ldots,(i_{L},t_{L})\} ordered by time t1<t2<⋯<tLt_{1}<t_{2}<\cdots<t_{L}. Each event contains an item imi_{m} and a Unix timestamp tm∈ℝ>0t_{m}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} measured in seconds. It may also include an interaction type or other semantic identifiers. The model predicts the next event autoregressively, and we take the prediction target to be the next item iL+1i_{L+1}.

A Transformer encoder maps each item imi_{m} to query, key, and value vectors 𝐪m,𝐤m,𝐯m∈ℝD\mathbf{q}_{m},\mathbf{k}_{m},\mathbf{v}_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. Standard RoPE (Su et al., 2024) acts on D/2D/2 2D rotation planes. In plane d∈{1,…,D/2}d\in\{1,\ldots,D/2\}, the 2D slice [𝐪m,2​d−1,𝐪m,2​d]⊤[\mathbf{q}_{m,2d-1},\mathbf{q}_{m,2d}]^{\top} is multiplied by a rotation matrix

𝐑⁡(ϕm)=[cos⁡ϕm−sin⁡ϕmsin⁡ϕmcos⁡ϕm].\mathbf{R}(\phi_{m})=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\phi_{m}&-\sin\phi_{m}\\ \sin\phi_{m}&\cos\phi_{m}\end{bmatrix}. (1)

The resulting dot product between rotated query and key in plane dd is

(𝐪m,d′)⊤​𝐤n,d′=(𝐪m,d)⊤​𝐑​(ϕn−ϕm)​𝐤n,d,(\mathbf{q}^{\prime}_{m,d})^{\top}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}_{n,d}=(\mathbf{q}_{m,d})^{\top}\mathbf{R}(\phi_{n}-\phi_{m})\mathbf{k}_{n,d}, (2)

which depends only on the angle difference (ϕn−ϕm)(\phi_{n}-\phi_{m}). Integer indices set ϕm=m​θd\phi_{m}=m\theta_{d}, where θd\theta_{d} is the fixed angular frequency of plane dd. So the angle difference becomes (n−m)​θd(n-m)\theta_{d} and the dot product depends only on the relative offset n−mn-m.

3 The T-RoPE Method

T-RoPE keeps RoPE’s computational interface but changes the meaning of the rotation, treating the user history as a timestamped event sequence rather than a text-like list. The construction has five parts: real-time rotation, learned per-layer scale coefficients, multiple temporal scales across dimensions, query alignment to the prediction time, and a key rotation that breaks the relative-time symmetry hiding calendar phase.

3.1 Timestamp-Based Rotation

Adjacent sequence positions are not equally spaced in time. In recommendation, neighboring events can be seconds, days, or months apart, yet the index mm treats every gap as an offset of one position (Figure 1a). T-RoPE therefore replaces the integer index with the absolute Unix timestamp tmt_{m} in seconds, used directly before rotation without centering or normalizing. As Figure 1b shows, events close in sequence index but far apart in time no longer occupy neighboring phases, while bursty events stay clustered. For dimension dd, the angle is ϕm,d=tm/βd\phi_{m,d}=t_{m}/\beta_{d}, where βd\beta_{d} is a base time frequency. Under this substitution the relative phase between two events becomes a function of their true temporal gap,

(𝐪m,d′)⊤​𝐤n,d′∝cos⁡(tn−tmβd),(\mathbf{q}^{\prime}_{m,d})^{\top}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}_{n,d}\propto\cos\!\left(\frac{t_{n}-t_{m}}{\beta_{d}}\right), (3)

so a large gap |tn−tm||t_{n}-t_{m}| weakens attention even between adjacent events in the truncated history.

3.2 Learnable Temporal Coefficients

Not all temporal scales deserve equal weight. Dominant cycles differ by domain and across layers within one model. Grocery purchases may follow cycles of 7 or 30 days, fashion demand may be seasonal, and marketplace activity may follow payday or promotion intervals. T-RoPE learns the strength of each cycle rather than fixing it.

To learn these strengths, T-RoPE introduces learnable coefficients αdq,αdk∈ℝ\alpha^{q}_{d},\alpha^{k}_{d}\in\mathbb{R}, separate for queries and keys,

ϕm,dq=αdq⋅tmβd,ϕn,dk=αdk⋅tnβd.\phi^{q}_{m,d}=\alpha^{q}_{d}\cdot\frac{t_{m}}{\beta_{d}},\qquad\phi^{k}_{n,d}=\alpha^{k}_{d}\cdot\frac{t_{n}}{\beta_{d}}. (4)

Independent query and key coefficients permit asymmetric specialization, but in practice we find the opposite. Across most dimensions the learned query and key coefficients align in both sign and magnitude, as Figure 3a shows, so both emphasize the same temporal bands. This alignment does not carry across layers, however. Figure 2 shows the per-layer RMS coefficient magnitude varying widely (a), and the temporal attention on the same sequence shifting substantially across the selected layers (b), so each layer learns its own temporal sensitivity rather than a single shared bias.

3.3 Multiscale Frequency Bank

A single base frequency resolves only one time scale, but user behavior spans many, from browsing sessions over minutes and household purchases over weeks or months to seasonal demand over a year. Capturing behavior across these scales requires several frequencies at once.

T-RoPE assigns a distinct base frequency βd\beta_{d} to each rotation plane dd using geometric spacing,

βd=exp[logβmin+d−1D/2−1(logβmax−logβmin)],d=1,…,D/2,\beta_{d}=\exp\!\left[\log\beta_{\min}+\frac{d-1}{D/2-1}\left(\log\beta_{\max}-\log\beta_{\min}\right)\right],\quad d=1,\ldots,D/2, (5)

where βmin\beta_{\min} and βmax\beta_{\max} are hyperparameters (defaults 10210^{2} and 10810^{8} seconds), giving a logarithmic bank from 10−210^{-2} to 10−810^{-8} radians/second. The bank fixes the available frequencies, and the learnable coefficients from Section 3.2 set how strongly each one contributes. As Figure 3 shows, even within a single layer training upweights a few temporal bands rather than all frequencies uniformly (a), and different frequencies lock onto different user cycles (b). The learned coefficients adjust the multiscale frequency bank so that the timestamp encoding can represent periodic patterns without explicitly encoding named calendar events such as Christmas.

3.4 Shifted Query Alignment

The rotation so far encodes when each history event occurred but not when the predicted event will occur. Since position mm is supervised to predict the event at tm+1t_{m+1} (and a deployed model receives the current time tnowt_{\text{now}} at inference), we adopt HSTU’s RAB Zhai et al. (2024) and rotate the query at this target time rather than at the history time. As illustrated in Figure 1c, T-RoPE assigns tm+1t_{m+1} to the query at position mm while keys keep their own timestamps,

ϕm,dq=αdq​tm+1βd,ϕn,dk=αdk​tnβd,\phi^{q}_{m,d}=\alpha^{q}_{d}\frac{t_{m+1}}{\beta_{d}},\quad\phi^{k}_{n,d}=\alpha^{k}_{d}\frac{t_{n}}{\beta_{d}}, (6)

which is implemented as a one-step shift of the timestamp-angle tensor along the sequence dimension. As Figure 4 shows, the final training position keeps its own timestamp since it serves only as a label, while at inference the final query slot instead receives the current session time tnowt_{\text{now}}, so the same item history can be evaluated under different prediction seasons (e.g., a holiday season versus a routine-replenishment context) without changing the architecture.

3.5 Non-Stationary Key Encoding

The preceding components give RoPE real timestamps, multiple scales, and the prediction-time query, but they keep one symmetry from standard RoPE. Because queries and keys rotate the same way, the dot product depends only on the angle difference ϕmq−ϕnk=(tm+1−tn)/βd\phi^{q}_{m}-\phi^{k}_{n}=(t_{m+1}-t_{n})/\beta_{d}, which a constant time shift leaves unchanged. The model can tell an item occurred seven days before the query but not where the query falls in the calendar cycle. T-RoPE removes this time-translation invariance next.

T-RoPE breaks this symmetry by applying the transpose of the standard rotation matrix to keys. For plane dd and key timestamp tnt_{n}, 𝐤n,d′=𝐑⁡(−ϕn,dk)​𝐤n,d=𝐑​(ϕn,dk)⊤​𝐤n,d\mathbf{k}^{\prime}_{n,d}=\mathbf{R}(-\phi^{k}_{n,d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}=\mathbf{R}(\phi^{k}_{n,d})^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{n,d}. Since 𝐑⁡(−ϕ)=𝐑​(ϕ)⊤\mathbf{R}(-\phi)=\mathbf{R}(\phi)^{\top} for 2D rotation matrices, this keeps the same norm-preserving rotation primitive while changing the phase relation inside attention. The resulting dot product is

(𝐪m,d′)⊤​𝐤n,d′=𝐪m,d⊤​𝐑​(−ϕm,dq)​𝐑​(−ϕn,dk)​𝐤n,d=𝐪m,d⊤​𝐑​(−(ϕm,dq+ϕn,dk))​𝐤n,d.(\mathbf{q}^{\prime}_{m,d})^{\top}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}_{n,d}=\mathbf{q}_{m,d}^{\top}\mathbf{R}(-\phi^{q}_{m,d})\mathbf{R}(-\phi^{k}_{n,d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}=\mathbf{q}_{m,d}^{\top}\mathbf{R}(-(\phi^{q}_{m,d}+\phi^{k}_{n,d}))\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}. (7)

The angle now depends on the sum (tm+1+tn)/βd(t_{m+1}+t_{n})/\beta_{d} rather than the gap, so attention shifts when the same history falls in a different calendar region. We prove in Section 4 that this is sufficient for absolute-time sensitivity.

3.6 Complete T-RoPE Formulation

Combining the components, each head receives a timestamp-aware, multiscale, prediction-aligned, and non-stationary rotation. The final T-RoPE rotated vectors are

𝐪m′=⨁d=1D/2𝐑⁡(ϕm,dq)​𝐪m,d,𝐤n′=⨁d=1D/2𝐑⁡(−ϕn,dk)​𝐤n,d,\mathbf{q}^{\prime}_{m}=\bigoplus_{d=1}^{D/2}\mathbf{R}(\phi^{q}_{m,d})\,\mathbf{q}_{m,d},\qquad\mathbf{k}^{\prime}_{n}=\bigoplus_{d=1}^{D/2}\mathbf{R}(-\phi^{k}_{n,d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}, (8)

where ⊕\oplus denotes concatenation over planes, giving the attention score

am​n=∑d=1D/2𝐪m,d⊤𝐑(−(αdqtm+1+αdktn)/βd)𝐤n,d.a_{mn}=\sum_{d=1}^{D/2}\mathbf{q}_{m,d}^{\top}\mathbf{R}(-(\alpha^{q}_{d}t_{m+1}+\alpha^{k}_{d}t_{n})/\beta_{d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}. (9)

This learned linear combination of the prediction timestamp tm+1t_{m+1} and the historical timestamp tnt_{n} across all planes lets T-RoPE represent both local recency and repeated temporal structure.

Due to space limits, the full forward and backward implementation of T-RoPE is deferred to Appendix B.1. The theoretical FLOP overhead (Appendix B.2) and measured latency (Appendix B.3) show that T-RoPE adds only cost linear in sequence length and head dimension.

4 Theoretical Analysis

We now isolate the property the method is meant to fix, namely whether the attention score can change when the same relative history is moved to a different calendar time, since a model that sees only temporal gaps can learn recency but cannot distinguish two queries at different phases of the same annual cycle. The argument proceeds in three steps. We first define time-translation invariance as the property that shifting every timestamp equally leaves attention unchanged; show that standard RoPE stays invariant even on timestamps when query and key share the same relative geometry; and show that T-RoPE’s non-stationary key breaks this symmetry, making periodic calendar effects representable. Full proofs and the supporting remarks are deferred to Appendix A.

Definition 1 (Time-translation invariance).

A positional encoding is time-translation invariant if, for all fixed item embedding vectors 𝐪,𝐤\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k} and all constant offsets c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R},

Attn​(𝐪,𝐤,tm+1,tn)=Attn​(𝐪,𝐤,tm+1+c,tn+c).\text{Attn}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k};t_{m+1},t_{n})=\text{Attn}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k};t_{m+1}+c,\,t_{n}+c).

This definition captures the exact limitation we want to avoid. If it holds, attention can depend on the elapsed time between query and key, but it cannot depend on the absolute calendar phase shared by both timestamps.

Theorem 1 (Shared-coefficient timestamp RoPE is time-translation invariant).

Let RoPE be applied with any fixed base frequencies {βd}\{\beta_{d}\} and any learnable shared coefficients αd=αdq=αdk\alpha_{d}=\alpha^{q}_{d}=\alpha^{k}_{d}. Suppose the timestamp-based angles are ϕm,dq=αd​tm+1/βd\phi^{q}_{m,d}=\alpha_{d}\,t_{m+1}/\beta_{d} and ϕn,dk=αd​tn/βd\phi^{k}_{n,d}=\alpha_{d}\,t_{n}/\beta_{d}, and the key uses the standard rotation 𝐤n,d′=𝐑⁡(ϕn,dk)​𝐤n,d\mathbf{k}^{\prime}_{n,d}=\mathbf{R}(\phi^{k}_{n,d})\mathbf{k}_{n,d}. Then Attn⁡(𝐪,𝐤,tm+1,tn)\mathrm{Attn}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k};\,t_{m+1},t_{n}) depends only on (tm+1−tn)(t_{m+1}-t_{n}).

The theorem explains why timestamp substitution alone is insufficient. In each plane the query–key dot product reduces to a rotation by αd​(tn−tm+1)/βd\alpha_{d}(t_{n}-t_{m+1})/\beta_{d}, which depends only on the gap and is unchanged by a common shift. Timestamp RoPE can measure how far a past event is from the prediction time, but it still erases the shared calendar location of the two timestamps.

Remark 1 (Independent standard-RoPE coefficients).

The same phase analysis shows that unequal coefficients can also break the symmetry, so the condition above is not the only route. Independent query and key coefficients can also break invariance. Our claim is only that T-RoPE’s non-stationary key is a RoPE-compatible sufficient mechanism that does so directly.

Theorem 2 (T-RoPE with non-stationary keys has absolute-time sensitivity).

Under T-RoPE, each per-plane summand of the attention score (Eq. 9) rotates by the angle −(αdqtm+1+αdktn)/βd-(\alpha^{q}_{d}\,t_{m+1}+\alpha^{k}_{d}\,t_{n})/\beta_{d}, which combines tm+1t_{m+1} and tnt_{n} additively. If the trained model satisfies αdq+αdk≠0\alpha^{q}_{d}+\alpha^{k}_{d}\neq 0 for dimension dd, then T-RoPE is not time-translation invariant. For any shift cc satisfying (αdq+αdk)​c/βd∉2​π​ℤ(\alpha^{q}_{d}+\alpha^{k}_{d})c/\beta_{d}\notin 2\pi\mathbb{Z}, there exist timestamps tm+1,tnt_{m+1},t_{n} and query and key vectors such that Attn⁡(tm+1,tn)≠Attn⁡(tm+1+c,tn+c)\mathrm{Attn}(t_{m+1},t_{n})\neq\mathrm{Attn}(t_{m+1}+c,t_{n}+c).

Unlike Theorem 1, the non-stationary key turns the per-plane phase into the sum (αdq​tm+1+αdk​tn)/βd(\alpha^{q}_{d}t_{m+1}+\alpha^{k}_{d}t_{n})/\beta_{d} rather than a difference, so a common shift moves it by (αdq+αdk)​c/βd(\alpha^{q}_{d}+\alpha^{k}_{d})c/\beta_{d} and the score changes unless this is a multiple of 2​π2\pi. Because the coefficients are learnable per dimension, the model chooses which timescales stay stationary and which become absolute-time sensitive, and in our deployed model this induces visible layer-dependent temporal bias (Figure 2) rather than the degenerate αdq=−αdk\alpha^{q}_{d}=-\alpha^{k}_{d} case. Absolute-time sensitivity matters because many recommendation signals are periodic, which the next corollary connects to calendar cycles.

Corollary 1 (Seasonality representability).

Let P>0P>0 be a temporal period (e.g., 365 days), and define the effective query angular frequency ωdq=αdq/βd\omega^{q}_{d}=\alpha^{q}_{d}/\beta_{d}. T-RoPE can represent a sinusoidal dependence on the prediction-time calendar phase with period PP if there exists a dimension dd and nonzero integer harmonic rr such that ωdq=2​π​r/P\omega^{q}_{d}=2\pi r/P.

Intuitively, with the key timestamp fixed the plane-dd score carries a cos⁡(αdq​tm+1/βd+const)\cos(\alpha^{q}_{d}t_{m+1}/\beta_{d}+\text{const}) term, so choosing ωdq=2​π​r/P\omega^{q}_{d}=2\pi r/P makes attention periodic in the prediction time with period PP.

5 Experiments

We evaluate T-RoPE in three settings. First, public benchmarks across domains and sizes test general accuracy. Second, a Shop ablation isolates which temporal mechanisms matter under non-stationary commerce. Third, an online A/B test measures production retrieval and business impact.

5.1 Validating T-RoPE on Public Datasets

To validate T-RoPE against existing methods with reproducible results, we evaluate on five public recommendation benchmarks whose statistics are listed in Table 6 (Appendix C). We compare against five existing methods: SASRec (Kang and McAuley, 2018) (no temporal encoding), TiSASRec (Li et al., 2020) (time-interval attention biases), HSTU (Zhai et al., 2024) (position-only RAB), HSTU + Time RAB (Zhai et al., 2024), and HSTU + TO-RoPE (Wei et al., 2025) (HSTU with Time+Pos RAB + TO-RoPE). All of these, together with our HSTU + T-RoPE (HSTU with Time+Pos RAB and T-RoPE), are implemented in the same PyTorch training framework and share identical item-ID inputs, preprocessing filters, maximum sequence lengths, leave-one-out protocol, candidate evaluation procedure, and training hyperparameters, making the comparison fair and consistent. Full hyperparameter settings are reported in Appendix D.

Detailed results across the five benchmarks are reported in Table 2, covering HR@10, HR@50, NDCG@10, NDCG@50, and MRR. HSTU + T-RoPE achieves the best result on all five metrics on every dataset, and the improvement scales with how much temporal structure the data contain. On the dense ML-20M benchmark, whose histories are fairly regular, gains are modest but consistent. The effect is clearer on sparse and commercial data, where T-RoPE improves over HSTU + Time RAB by 8–12% across all five metrics on Amazon Books, and over TO-RoPE by 78–130% in HR@10 and 72–112% in HR@50 across the PixelRec splits. The largest margins appear on the sparse and commercial data, where absolute calendar phase carries the most signal.

5.2 Ablation Study on an Industrial-Scale Dataset

To identify which design choices drive the gains, we ablate T-RoPE components on Shop, an internal e-commerce dataset with roughly 150M users, 4.8M items, and over 6B interactions spanning multiple years. Larger and more temporally heterogeneous than the public benchmarks, it better tests the multiscale and non-stationary mechanisms. The model uses 128-dimensional embeddings, 12 HSTU blocks, 8 attention heads, 32 attention dimensions per head, and a maximum sequence length of 512. We use a one-day temporal holdout (training on interactions before the holdout date, every meaningful interaction on the held-out day counting as a positive) and report recall@K rather than HR@K, since a user may have several relevant interactions. The detailed results are shown in Table 3, which removes components cumulatively from the full T-RoPE model down to the HSTU + Time RAB backbone, with the key findings discussed below.

The multiscale frequency bank and shifted queries supply the core gains.

The multiscale bank has the largest effect. Removing it cuts NDCG@50 by 36% when comparing rows 3 and 4. This shows that multiscale rotation turns raw timestamps into usable frequency structure. Without it, the timestamp is just noise, and the single frequency embedding in row 4 falls about 4% below the HSTU + Time RAB backbone in row 5. Shifted query alignment provides the next largest gain by adding seasonality to the query at inference. It improves NDCG@50 by 7% when comparing rows 2 and 3.

The non-stationary key drives absolute-time sensitivity, complemented by key and query rotation.

Adding the non-stationary key (§3.5, row 1) outperforms the shifted model (row 2) on all five metrics, improving recall@200 by 3.2% and NDCG@50 by 4.2%, which confirms that it injects useful absolute-time sensitivity. Key and query rotation each carry such sensitivity on their own (Remark 1), so we further ablate them one at a time. The shifted-query rotation has the larger effect on retrieval, since removing it (row 6) lowers recall@200 by 3.0%, whereas removing the key rotation (row 7) instead costs ranking precision, cutting NDCG@50 by 10.3%. The two are therefore complementary, and the non-stationary key combines both sides and pushes furthest.

Time RAB and T-RoPE are complementary.

Removing Time RAB from the full model (row 8) lowers all metrics, with the starkest drop of 27.0% in MRR. This suggests RAB still captures useful relative-recency signals that T-RoPE does not. Even so, T-RoPE without RAB still improves NDCG@50 by roughly 50% over the baseline, so the two mechanisms contribute independently and combine for the best result.

5.3 Online A/B Test

To measure real production impact, we deploy T-RoPE in an online A/B test in the Shop app recommender, scaling up the offline architecture while keeping the T-RoPE design unchanged. Table 4 reports relative lift against the production control, an identical model without T-RoPE.

The online results align with the offline gains. CVR shows the strongest signal (+0.33%+0.33\%, p=0.037p=0.037), indicating that time-aware retrieval converts more sessions into interactions. This carries to higher-intent behavior. The Shop orders also increase +0.63%+0.63\% (p=0.094p=0.094), directional evidence of downstream value. Overall, time-aware RoPE yields positive business gains in production.

6 Related Work

Sequential recommendation models

Sequential recommendation models user preferences from ordered interaction histories. Early deep models used recurrent networks (GRU4Rec (Hidasi et al., 2016), NARM (Li et al., 2017)) and convolution (Caser (Tang and Wang, 2018)). The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) reshaped the field: SASRec (Kang and McAuley, 2018) showed that unidirectional self-attention outperforms RNNs, and BERT4Rec (Sun et al., 2019) added bidirectional masked-item prediction. Later work enriched attention with item attributes (FDSA (Zhang et al., 2019)), replaced it with learnable frequency-domain filters (FMLP-Rec (Zhou et al., 2022)), or added self-supervised pretraining (S3-Rec (Zhou et al., 2020)); at production scale, HSTU (Zhai et al., 2024) reaches trillions of parameters via hierarchical action-based transduction. A newer thread casts recommendation as autoregressive generation over discrete semantic tokens: TIGER (Rajput et al., 2023) uses RQ-VAE item codes, LETTER (Wang et al., 2024) adds collaborative signals to tokenization, ActionPiece (Hou et al., 2025) tokenizes at action granularity, PSID (Zhang et al., 2025) relies on pure semantic IDs, and HLLM (Chen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026a; He et al., 2026) pairs an item-level with a user-level LLM. T-RoPE is a drop-in positional encoding compatible with any of these Transformer backbones.

Temporal information in sequential recommendation

Temporal dynamics are a core problem in sequential recommendation. Early collaborative filtering showed that preferences and item popularity shift substantially over calendar time (Koren, 2009). TiSASRec (Li et al., 2020) discretizes the elapsed gap |ti−tj||t_{i}-t_{j}| into buckets injected as additive attention biases, capturing relative recency but only the gap magnitude, with no calendar-phase awareness. Knowledge-guided methods (Wang et al., 2020) learn time-decay kernels over item relations, and attention-mixture approaches (Tran et al., 2023) condition on calendar features such as hour of day. TO-RoPE (Wei et al., 2025) blends position indices and timestamps inside RoPE angles, making attention sensitive to temporal distance, but because query and key share the same timestamp coefficient it remains time-translation invariant (Theorem 1, Remark 2). T-RoPE instead introduces a non-stationary key with learnable query/key coefficients, breaking that invariance and giving the absolute-time awareness needed for periodic patterns such as seasonal purchase cycles.

7 Conclusion

We introduced T-RoPE, a time-aware rotary embedding that rotates attention by when events happen rather than by their order, so the model reasons directly over elapsed time and recurring calendar cycles. We proved that shared-geometry timestamp encodings are time-translation invariant and cannot model seasonal preferences, motivating T-RoPE’s non-stationary keys. We validated it on public benchmarks and a large commercial dataset, where it consistently outperforms baselines, with the largest gains under high temporal heterogeneity. Grounding rotary attention in time is thus principled and effective for recommendation.

AI use statement

We used AI only to aid and polish writing at the sentence level, including edits to clarity, grammar, and phrasing. We did not use generative AI for literature retrieval or discovery, research ideation, theoretical development, methodology or experiment design, code implementation, data generation or processing, data analysis, or interpretation of results. The authors reviewed every AI-assisted edit and take full responsibility for the final content of this work.

Ethics statement

Public experiments used established recommendation benchmarks obtained from the cited sources. The industrial experiments use data for which the authors had authorized access, and the online experiment compared two recommender variants in the normal operation of the Shop app. The industrial and online studies followed the company’s processes for data access, privacy, and experimentation governance. We report their results only in aggregate and release neither individual user records nor personally identifying information. The proprietary data and production infrastructure therefore cannot be made public.

Reproducibility statement

We support reproduction of the public-benchmark results through the complete method specification in Section 3, the experimental protocol in Section 5.1, and the implementation details in Appendix B. Appendix B.1 gives forward and backward algorithms, Appendix C lists the public datasets and their statistics, and Appendix D reports the architecture, optimization settings, random seed, and hardware. Appendix A contains full proofs of the theoretical claims, while Appendices B.2 and B.3 document computational cost and measured throughput.

Appendix A Full Proofs

A.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Restatement. With shared coefficients αd=αdq=αdk\alpha_{d}=\alpha^{q}_{d}=\alpha^{k}_{d} and angles ϕm,dq=αd​tm+1/βd\phi^{q}_{m,d}=\alpha_{d}t_{m+1}/\beta_{d}, ϕn,dk=αd​tn/βd\phi^{k}_{n,d}=\alpha_{d}t_{n}/\beta_{d} under the standard key rotation 𝐤n,d′=𝐑⁡(ϕn,dk)​𝐤n,d\mathbf{k}^{\prime}_{n,d}=\mathbf{R}(\phi^{k}_{n,d})\mathbf{k}_{n,d}, the attention score depends only on (tm+1−tn)(t_{m+1}-t_{n}) and is therefore time-translation invariant.

Proof.

We give the full argument for standard key rotation with shared query and key timestamp coefficients αdq=αdk≜αd\alpha^{q}_{d}=\alpha^{k}_{d}\triangleq\alpha_{d}.

Standard RoPE with ϕm,dq=αd​tm+1/βd\phi^{q}_{m,d}=\alpha_{d}t_{m+1}/\beta_{d} and ϕn,dk=αd​tn/βd\phi^{k}_{n,d}=\alpha_{d}t_{n}/\beta_{d} (standard key rotation 𝐑⁡(ϕn,dk)\mathbf{R}(\phi^{k}_{n,d})) gives

(𝐪m,d′)⊤​𝐤n,d′\displaystyle(\mathbf{q}^{\prime}_{m,d})^{\top}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}_{n,d} =𝐪m,d⊤​𝐑​(ϕn,dk−ϕm,dq)​𝐤n,d=𝐪m,d⊤​𝐑​(αd​(tn−tm+1)/βd)​𝐤n,d,\displaystyle=\mathbf{q}_{m,d}^{\top}\mathbf{R}(\phi^{k}_{n,d}-\phi^{q}_{m,d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}=\mathbf{q}_{m,d}^{\top}\mathbf{R}(\alpha_{d}(t_{n}-t_{m+1})/\beta_{d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d},

which depends only on (tn−tm+1)(t_{n}-t_{m+1}). Summing over planes and heads preserves time-translation invariance.

For comparison, if standard key rotation uses independent coefficients αdq\alpha^{q}_{d} and αdk\alpha^{k}_{d}, the phase is

ϕn,dk−ϕm,dq=(αdk​tn−αdq​tm+1)/βd.\phi^{k}_{n,d}-\phi^{q}_{m,d}=(\alpha^{k}_{d}t_{n}-\alpha^{q}_{d}t_{m+1})/\beta_{d}.

Under a global shift by cc, the phase changes by (αdk−αdq)​c/βd(\alpha^{k}_{d}-\alpha^{q}_{d})c/\beta_{d}. Therefore this standard-RoPE family is invariant only for active planes where αdq=αdk\alpha^{q}_{d}=\alpha^{k}_{d}. Opposite nonzero coefficients depend on the timestamp sum and are not time-translation invariant. ∎

Remark 2 (Relation to TO-RoPE).

The same argument covers the timestamp component of TO-RoPE, which shares one timestamp coefficient across query and key. That component depends only on (τm−τn)(\tau_{m}-\tau_{n}) and is therefore time-translation invariant, so it cannot represent seasonal shifts on its own.

A.2 Proof of Theorem 2

Restatement. Under T-RoPE the per-plane attention equals 𝐪m,d⊤𝐑(−(αdqtm+1+αdktn)/βd)𝐤n,d\mathbf{q}_{m,d}^{\top}\mathbf{R}(-(\alpha^{q}_{d}t_{m+1}+\alpha^{k}_{d}t_{n})/\beta_{d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}; if αdq+αdk≠0\alpha^{q}_{d}+\alpha^{k}_{d}\neq 0 for some dimension dd, then T-RoPE is not time-translation invariant.

Proof.

We expand Eq. 7 carefully using the rotation group property 𝐑⁡(a)​𝐑​(b)=𝐑⁡(a+b)\mathbf{R}(a)\mathbf{R}(b)=\mathbf{R}(a+b),

(𝐪m,d′)⊤​𝐤n,d′\displaystyle(\mathbf{q}^{\prime}_{m,d})^{\top}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}_{n,d} =(𝐑⁡(ϕm,dq)​𝐪m,d)⊤​(𝐑⁡(−ϕn,dk)​𝐤n,d)\displaystyle=\left(\mathbf{R}(\phi^{q}_{m,d})\mathbf{q}_{m,d}\right)^{\top}\left(\mathbf{R}(-\phi^{k}_{n,d})\mathbf{k}_{n,d}\right)
=𝐪m,d⊤​𝐑​(ϕm,dq)⊤​𝐑​(−ϕn,dk)​𝐤n,d\displaystyle=\mathbf{q}_{m,d}^{\top}\mathbf{R}(\phi^{q}_{m,d})^{\top}\mathbf{R}(-\phi^{k}_{n,d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}
=𝐪m,d⊤​𝐑​(−ϕm,dq)​𝐑​(−ϕn,dk)​𝐤n,d\displaystyle=\mathbf{q}_{m,d}^{\top}\mathbf{R}(-\phi^{q}_{m,d})\mathbf{R}(-\phi^{k}_{n,d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}
=𝐪m,d⊤​𝐑​(−ϕm,dq−ϕn,dk)​𝐤n,d.\displaystyle=\mathbf{q}_{m,d}^{\top}\mathbf{R}(-\phi^{q}_{m,d}-\phi^{k}_{n,d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}.

Substituting ϕm,dq=αdq​tm+1/βd\phi^{q}_{m,d}=\alpha^{q}_{d}t_{m+1}/\beta_{d} and ϕn,dk=αdk​tn/βd\phi^{k}_{n,d}=\alpha^{k}_{d}t_{n}/\beta_{d} gives

(𝐪m,d′)⊤𝐤n,d′=𝐪m,d⊤𝐑(−(αdqtm+1+αdktn)/βd)𝐤n,d.(\mathbf{q}^{\prime}_{m,d})^{\top}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}_{n,d}=\mathbf{q}_{m,d}^{\top}\mathbf{R}(-(\alpha^{q}_{d}t_{m+1}+\alpha^{k}_{d}t_{n})/\beta_{d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}.

Under the time shift (tm+1,tn)→(tm+1+c,tn+c)(t_{m+1},t_{n})\to(t_{m+1}+c,t_{n}+c), the argument changes by (αdq+αdk)​c/βd(\alpha^{q}_{d}+\alpha^{k}_{d})c/\beta_{d}. If (αdq+αdk)​c/βd∉2​π​ℤ(\alpha^{q}_{d}+\alpha^{k}_{d})c/\beta_{d}\notin 2\pi\mathbb{Z}, the shifted and unshifted rotation matrices are different. Since two different rotation matrices define different bilinear forms, there exist nondegenerate vectors 𝐪m,d\mathbf{q}_{m,d} and 𝐤n,d\mathbf{k}_{n,d} for which the dot product changes after the shift. This gives a counterexample to the universal equality required by time-translation invariance. If the phase shift is in 2​π​ℤ2\pi\mathbb{Z}, that particular shift can coincide, but such modulo coincidences do not establish invariance for all shifts. ∎

Remark 3 (Learnable degeneracy and timescale selection).

The condition αdq+αdk≠0\alpha^{q}_{d}+\alpha^{k}_{d}\neq 0 for some dd is genuinely needed. If training converges to αdq=−αdk\alpha^{q}_{d}=-\alpha^{k}_{d} for all dd, T-RoPE degenerates to the time-translation invariant case. This is not purely a failure mode, since learnable per-dimension coefficients let the model choose which timescales stay stationary and which become absolute-time sensitive. In our deployed model the degenerate case does not arise, and the learned coefficients induce visible layer-dependent temporal bias (Figure 2).

A.3 Proof of Corollary 1

Restatement. For a period P>0P>0 and effective query angular frequency ωdq=αdq/βd\omega^{q}_{d}=\alpha^{q}_{d}/\beta_{d}, T-RoPE can represent a sinusoidal dependence on the prediction-time calendar phase with period PP whenever ωdq=2​π​r/P\omega^{q}_{d}=2\pi r/P for some dimension dd and nonzero integer harmonic rr.

Proof.

The attention in dimension dd can be written as

fd(tm+1,tn)=𝐪m,d⊤𝐑(−(αdqtm+1+αdktn)/βd)𝐤n,d.f_{d}(t_{m+1},t_{n})=\mathbf{q}_{m,d}^{\top}\mathbf{R}(-(\alpha^{q}_{d}t_{m+1}+\alpha^{k}_{d}t_{n})/\beta_{d})\,\mathbf{k}_{n,d}.

Expanding in terms of cos\cos and sin\sin,

fd=(q1​k1+q2​k2)​cos⁡(αdq​tm+1+αdk​tnβd)+(q2​k1−q1​k2)​sin⁡(αdq​tm+1+αdk​tnβd).f_{d}=(q_{1}k_{1}+q_{2}k_{2})\cos\!\left(\frac{\alpha^{q}_{d}t_{m+1}+\alpha^{k}_{d}t_{n}}{\beta_{d}}\right)+(q_{2}k_{1}-q_{1}k_{2})\sin\!\left(\frac{\alpha^{q}_{d}t_{m+1}+\alpha^{k}_{d}t_{n}}{\beta_{d}}\right).

Holding tnt_{n} fixed, the key term αdk​tn/βd\alpha^{k}_{d}t_{n}/\beta_{d} is a constant phase offset. Let ωdq=αdq/βd\omega^{q}_{d}=\alpha^{q}_{d}/\beta_{d}. If ωdq=2​π​r/P\omega^{q}_{d}=2\pi r/P for a nonzero integer harmonic rr, then both the sine and cosine terms are periodic in tm+1t_{m+1} with period PP. Thus T-RoPE has the capacity to express sinusoidal modulation over prediction time at the target calendar period. ∎

Appendix B Implementation Details

B.1 Forward and backward algorithms

Each layer using T-RoPE maintains a geometric frequency bank β∈ℝD/2\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{D/2} and two trainable coefficient vectors αq,αk∈ℝD/2\alpha^{q},\alpha^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{D/2}. The frequency bank uses βmin=102\beta_{\min}=10^{2} seconds and βmax=108\beta_{\max}=10^{8} seconds by default, and the coefficients are initialized independently from 𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) with σ=1.0\sigma=1.0.

Algorithm 1 expands the forward pass. Because we use absolute Unix timestamps in seconds, which are on the order of 10910^{9}, T-RoPE computes Φq\Phi^{q} and Φk\Phi^{k} in FP32 even when the surrounding model uses BF16. The rotated outputs are cast back to the model dtype after the trigonometric functions have been evaluated.

Algorithm 3 summarizes the custom autograd path used for learnable angles. A fixed RoPE backward only needs d​XdX, which is obtained by applying the conjugate rotation to the upstream gradient. T-RoPE additionally returns d​Φd\Phi because Φ\Phi depends on trainable coefficients. This is the main computational difference from raw RoPE.

The gradients for the learnable coefficients follow directly from Φb,l,dq=αdq​tb,lq/βd\Phi^{q}_{b,l,d}=\alpha^{q}_{d}t^{q}_{b,l}/\beta_{d} and Φb,l,dk=αdk​tb,l/βd\Phi^{k}_{b,l,d}=\alpha^{k}_{d}t_{b,l}/\beta_{d},

∂ℒ∂αdq=∑b,l∂ℒ∂Φb,l,dq​tb,lqβd,∂ℒ∂αdk=∑b,l∂ℒ∂Φb,l,dk​tb,lβd,\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\alpha^{q}_{d}}=\sum_{b,l}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi^{q}_{b,l,d}}\frac{t^{q}_{b,l}}{\beta_{d}},\qquad\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\alpha^{k}_{d}}=\sum_{b,l}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi^{k}_{b,l,d}}\frac{t_{b,l}}{\beta_{d}}, (10)

where tb,lq=tb,l+1t^{q}_{b,l}=t_{b,l+1} for l<Ll<L and tb,Lq=tb,Lt^{q}_{b,L}=t_{b,L} under the shifted query boundary rule. Because tb,l+1t_{b,l+1} is a Unix timestamp measured in seconds, the gradients are usually large and must be clipped or rescaled to stabilize training.

B.2 Parameter and FLOP overhead

Let BB be the batch size and LL the sequence length, so N=B​LN=BL is the total number of tokens. Let HH be the number of attention heads, DD the per-head dimension, P=D/2P=D/2 the number of rotary planes (each plane is a 2×22\times 2 rotation over one channel pair), and MM the number of Transformer layers that use T-RoPE. Because each T-RoPE module keeps separate query and key coefficients, it adds 2​P=D2P=D learnable parameters, so the full model adds M​DMD parameters in total. In our HSTU experiments (M=2M=2 layers, D=128D=128), this is only 2⋅128=2562\cdot 128=256 additional parameters.

We count multiply, add/subtract, and divide as one FLOP each, and report sin\sin and cos\cos separately as transcendental operations. The non-stationary key rotation has the same arithmetic count as a standard rotation. It only changes signs in the rotation equations. The rotation cost below corresponds to Algorithm 2 applied once to QQ and once to KK.

Operation Arithmetic FLOPs Transcendental ops
Build Φq,Φk\Phi^{q},\Phi^{k} 4​N​P4NP –
Rotate Q,KQ,K 12​N​H​P12NHP 2​N​P2NP sin\sin and 2​N​P2NP cos\cos
Fixed-RoPE backward d​Q,d​KdQ,dK 12​N​H​P12NHP 2​N​P2NP sin\sin and 2​N​P2NP cos\cos
Extra learnable-angle d​Φd\Phi 18​N​H​P+2​N​P​(H−1)18NHP+2NP(H-1) –
Coefficient gradients ≈4​N​P\approx 4NP –

Thus, relative to raw RoPE with a fixed precomputed rotation cache, T-RoPE adds 4​N​P4NP forward arithmetic FLOPs to build timestamp-dependent angles, plus runtime trigonometric evaluations if the kernel computes sin⁡Φ\sin\Phi and cos⁡Φ\cos\Phi on the fly. During training, the extra cost over fixed raw RoPE is the d​Φd\Phi computation and reduction, followed by the coefficient-gradient chain above. These extra terms are linear in sequence length and head dimension, while self-attention remains quadratic in sequence length.

B.3 Static latency analysis.

Table 5 reports static latency based on sampled training and validation iterator throughput during the second epoch for the Pixel1M and Shop examples. T-RoPE has modest observed throughput overhead relative to baseline HSTU and is comparable to TO-RoPE.

Appendix C Dataset Statistics

Table 6 reports the size of the five public benchmarks used in Section 5.1.

Appendix D Hyperparameter Settings

Table 7 summarises the architecture and training hyperparameters. All models use 2 Transformer blocks, 128 in-batch negatives, and a learning rate of 10−310^{-3}. The values shown are the defaults shared by ML-20M, Amazon Books, Pixel200K, Pixel1M, and Pixel8M. The sequence-length exception is listed in the footnote. Here dd is the embedding dimension, HH the number of attention heads, AA the attention dimension, and RAB the relative attention bucket type (Pos = position only; T+P = time + position); “—” denotes an absent component.

For public benchmark training, we use AdamW with learning rate 10−310^{-3}, betas (0.9,0.98)(0.9,0.98), weight decay 0.0010.001, batch size 128128, seed 4242, and dropout 0.20.2 for all dropout settings. Models are trained for at least 10 and at most 100 epochs, with a ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler on validation HR@10. The objective is SampledSoftmaxLoss with 128 sampled negatives and temperature 0.050.05. Histories are truncated to the dataset maximum sequence length. All public training and evaluation runs use a single NVIDIA H100.

Appendix E Additional Visualizations

The output attention of T-RoPE is visualized in Figure 5, which shows that the day-, week-, month-, and year-scale event blocks become increasingly grouped by their real time spacing as each component is added, until full T-RoPE cleanly separates the blocks by elapsed time.
